# Embedding-Space Drift Under Fine-Tuning: How Quickly Models Forget Their Pretraining Geometry

## 1. Executive Summary

**Question.** How fast does domain fine-tuning destroy the local neighbourhood structure of a pretrained LM's
representation space? Does that speed depend on model scale and on the fine-tuning domain? And can neighbourhood
loss serve as an early warning of catastrophic forgetting?

**What we did.** We ran 22 fine-tuning runs (6 base models from 160M to 3B parameters, two model families, medical / code /
general-text domains, up to 3,000 steps, 3 seeds for the main small-model conditions, plus learning-rate and
full-fine-tuning ablations). We evaluated each run at 17 checkpoints on four kinds of measure:
- k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) preservation of 1,000 held-out general-text probes;
- three isotropy measures;
- general knowledge (MMLU + ARC-Easy, 1,070 items);
- WikiText perplexity.

**Key findings.** Three of the four sub-hypotheses are not supported as stated, and the fourth only partly.
- **H1 (speed vs. scale): partly supported.** Larger models do keep more of their geometry at a given step:
  preservation@10 at step 500 was 0.42 for Pythia-160M, then 0.74 (410M), 0.79 (Qwen-0.5B), 0.82 (1.5B) and
  0.85 (3B) on medical text.
  - "Below 50 % within 500 steps for sub-1B models" held for Pythia-160M (it crossed after ~90–220 steps) but
    not for Qwen2.5-0.5B. That model never fell below 0.71 in 3,000 steps at the standard LoRA learning rate.
  - The crossing step depends mainly on the size of the updates. The same 0.5B model crossed 0.5 at ~420–500
    steps with a 5× larger learning rate.
  - The 7B part of H1 could not be tested: the only GPU slice large enough was shared and the run OOM'd. The
    largest model we tested (3B) was still at 0.83 at step 1,000.
- **H2 (isotropy falls monotonically): not supported.** No run (0/20) showed a monotone loss of isotropy on any
  of the three measures. The net change was small (median −7 % IsoScore, −5 % effective rank, +1.7 % mean
  cosine) and non-monotone, and Pythia-160M first became *more* isotropic.
- **H3 (accuracy starts dropping below 60 % preservation): not supported as a threshold.**
  - Preservation is strongly associated with forgetting overall (Spearman ρ = 0.70 with Δ general-knowledge
    accuracy; ρ = −0.88 with Δ WikiText NLL).
  - But in Qwen models general-knowledge accuracy dropped significantly (McNemar p < 0.05) while preservation
    was still 0.77–0.90. Up to 10 pp of MMLU+ARC accuracy was lost without ever reaching 0.6.
  - So 0.6 is far too late to be an early warning. The level of preservation at which forgetting begins also
    differs between model families.
- **H4 (medical preserves more than code): not supported; the reverse holds for most models.** For Qwen-0.5B
  (3 seeds) and Pythia-410M, code fine-tuning kept *more* general-text geometry than medical fine-tuning.
  - Matched-checkpoint difference medical − code = −0.039, with medical higher at only 19 % of 128 checkpoints
    (Wilcoxon p = 1e-9). Code also caused less forgetting.
  - This held even though the clinical notes are lexically much closer to general text than code is (unigram
    JSD 0.45 vs 0.63 bits).
  - Only Pythia-160M followed H4's direction.
  - Which domain drifted less matched how familiar each domain already was to the base model (base NLL on code
    is much lower than on clinical notes), not vocabulary overlap.

**Practical implication.** kNN preservation on a fixed probe set is a cheap, label-free signal that tracks
general-LM degradation (perplexity) very closely within a model family. But it is not a universal
"forgetting thermometer" with a fixed 60 % threshold. A practical monitor would be a family- and recipe-specific
calibration, or simply the *rate* of preservation loss.

## 2. Research Question & Motivation

Fine-tuning a pretrained LM on a narrow domain improves in-domain performance but erodes general abilities
(catastrophic forgetting). Running general-knowledge benchmarks at every checkpoint is expensive. Probing the
*geometry* of a model's representations on a fixed set of texts is cheap and needs no labels. If geometric drift
reliably precedes forgetting, it could be an early-warning monitor.

The hypothesis under test had four parts:
1. Neighbourhood preservation drops below 50 % within 500 steps for sub-1B models but only after 2,000+ steps
   for 7B models.
2. Isotropy decreases monotonically.
3. General-knowledge accuracy starts to decline once preservation falls below 60 %.
4. Medical fine-tuning preserves more structure than code because of greater vocabulary overlap with
   pretraining data.

**Gap.** No literature review was pre-gathered for this workspace (the resource-finder stage was skipped), so
this section rests on background knowledge. Prior work studies representation similarity after fine-tuning
(e.g. Merchant et al. 2020, CKA/SVCCA studies of BERT), anisotropy of contextual embeddings (Ethayarajh 2019;
Mu & Viswanath 2018; IsoScore, Rudman et al. 2022), and forgetting under LLM fine-tuning (Luo et al. 2023;
Kalajdzievski 2024; Biderman et al. 2024 "LoRA learns less and forgets less"). Those studies mostly measure end
states. Our contribution is a *step-resolved* study (17 checkpoints) that links local neighbourhood structure to
item-level forgetting tests across scale, domain and training recipe.

## 3. Experimental Setup

### Models
Base (non-instruct) checkpoints, loaded locally:
- **Qwen2.5 family** (one tokenizer and pretraining corpus): Qwen2.5-0.5B, -1.5B and -3B.
- **Pythia family** (trained on the Pile): Pythia-160M and -410M, a second family below 1B.

Qwen2.5-7B was downloaded and started, but the run was abandoned (see §6).

### Fine-tuning recipe (identical across sizes)
- **Method:** LoRA with r = 64, α = 128, no dropout, on every linear layer (attention q/k/v/o + MLP; for
  GPT-NeoX: query_key_value, dense, dense_h_to_4h, dense_4h_to_h).
- **Optimiser:** AdamW, β = (0.9, 0.95), learning rate 2e-4, 50-step linear warm-up then constant, gradient
  clipping at 1.0.
- **Batch and length:** batch 4 × 512 tokens (2,048 tokens/step), 3,000 steps (6.1M tokens).
- **Precision:** bf16 base weights with gradient checkpointing. The next-token loss is computed in 256-token
  chunks with recomputation so the run fits 2–5 GB GPU slices.
- Seed 1 everywhere, plus seeds 2 and 3 for the main small-model conditions. The seed controls document order
  and LoRA initialisation.

### Ablations
- Qwen2.5-0.5B LoRA with lr 1e-3 (5× larger), medical and code.
- Pythia-160M **full** fine-tuning (fp32 master weights, bf16 autocast, lr 1e-5), medical and code.

### Fine-tuning corpora
Texts are concatenated with EOS and cut into 512-token chunks. Each run uses a seeded prefix of ~6.1M tokens.
- **Medical:** Asclepius synthetic clinical notes (`starmpcc/Asclepius-Synthetic-Clinical-Notes`, 40k unique
  notes).
- **Code:** Python files from `codeparrot/codeparrot-clean-valid` (30k files, 800–20k characters, not
  auto-generated).
- **General (control):** WikiText-103 training paragraphs. This control separates "being fine-tuned at all"
  from "being moved to a new domain".

### Probe and evaluation sets
All are fixed and disjoint from training data (`src/prep_data.py`).
- **General probes:** 1,000 WikiText-103 test/validation paragraphs (≥ 400 characters), truncated to 128
  tokens. These are the primary probes. We also used 300 medical and 300 code probes from held-out documents.
- **Representation:** mean-pooled hidden states over token positions ≥ 1 (position 0 is an attention-sink
  token), taken at the middle layer and the final (post-norm) layer.
- **General knowledge:**
  - MMLU: 570 questions (10 per subject), 0-shot, argmax over next-token log-probabilities of " A".." D".
  - ARC-Easy: 500 test questions, acc_norm (choice log-likelihood divided by character length).
  - "GK" below is the pooled accuracy over all 1,070 items.
- **Language modelling:** NLL per token on 64 × 512 tokens of held-out WikiText (general) and of held-out
  in-domain text.

### Metrics (`src/metrics.py`)
All geometric metrics compare each checkpoint with step 0.
- **kNN preservation@k:** the mean, over probes, of |N_k^step0(i) ∩ N_k^t(i)| / k. Neighbourhoods use cosine
  similarity, k ∈ {5, 10, 20}, with k = 10 as the primary value. We also report a mean-centred variant, because
  raw cosines are dominated by a shared direction (mean pairwise cosine ≈ 0.83–0.86).
- **Linear CKA:** a global similarity measure.
- **Isotropy:**
  - mean pairwise cosine (anisotropy; higher = less isotropic);
  - IsoScore (Rudman et al. 2022);
  - effective rank (the exponential of the entropy of the covariance eigenvalues).

### Statistics (`src/analyze.py`)
- **Threshold crossings:** found by linear interpolation in log(1 + step).
- **Forgetting:** exact McNemar (binomial) test on the 1,070 items, each checkpoint against step 0.
- **H2 (isotropy):** Spearman correlation of each isotropy metric with step, plus the fraction of checkpoint
  transitions that move toward anisotropy.
- **H3 (threshold):** Mann–Whitney U test comparing Δ GK at checkpoints with preservation ≥ 0.6 against those
  below 0.6, plus Spearman correlations.
- **H4 (domain):** paired Wilcoxon test over checkpoints matched on (model, method, variant, seed, step).

### Hardware and cost
- 4× RTX A6000 (48 GB), heavily shared with other users. During the session there was usually 2–6 GB free per
  GPU, and one ~30 GB slice for part of the time.
- No API calls were made.
- Runtimes: Pythia-160M runs took 7–10 min; Qwen-0.5B runs took 20–26 min on a 5 GB slice. Qwen-1.5B and 3B
  managed only ~2.9–4.6 s/step plus 4–6 min per evaluation on the shared GPU, so their trajectories are
  truncated (see the tables).
- Software: Python 3.12.12, torch 2.14.1+cu130, transformers 5.20.2, peft 0.21.2, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1,
  pandas 3.1.0.

## 4. Results

### 4.1 H1 – Neighbourhood preservation by scale and step

kNN@10 preservation of general-text probes at the final layer. Values are means over seeds; the sd over the
three Qwen-0.5B seeds is ≤ 0.016 at every step shown.

| Model (recipe) | Domain | step 10 | 100 | 500 | 1000 | 2000 | 3000 | crosses 0.5 at |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pythia-160M LoRA (2 seeds) | medical | 0.89 | 0.57 | **0.42** | 0.46 | 0.36 | 0.31 | ~96–117 |
| Pythia-160M LoRA (2 seeds) | code | 0.89 | 0.60 | 0.55 | 0.42 | 0.31 | 0.28 | ~123–224 |
| Pythia-160M LoRA | general | 0.89 | 0.46 | 0.39 | 0.40 | 0.45 | 0.43 | ~90 |
| Pythia-160M full FT (lr 1e-5) | medical | 0.90 | 0.83 | 0.79 | 0.70 | 0.65 | 0.62 | never |
| Pythia-160M full FT (lr 1e-5) | code | 0.90 | 0.85 | 0.82 | 0.76 | 0.52 | 0.51 | never |
| Pythia-410M LoRA | medical | 0.93 | 0.80 | 0.74 | 0.72 | 0.71 | 0.71 | never |
| Pythia-410M LoRA | code | 0.93 | 0.87 | 0.81 | 0.76 | 0.76 | 0.74 | never |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B LoRA (3 seeds) | medical | 0.96 | 0.83 | 0.79 | 0.76 | 0.75 | 0.73 | never |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B LoRA (3 seeds) | code | 0.98 | 0.91 | 0.87 | 0.84 | 0.82 | 0.81 | never |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B LoRA | general | 0.92 | 0.81 | 0.79 | 0.77 | 0.76 | 0.76 | never |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B LoRA **lr 1e-3** | medical | 0.88 | 0.71 | 0.43 | 0.35 | 0.25 | 0.22 | ~420 |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B LoRA **lr 1e-3** | code | 0.95 | 0.78 | 0.50 | 0.37 | 0.28 | 0.27 | ~500 |
| Qwen2.5-1.5B LoRA | medical | 0.98 | 0.86 | 0.82 | 0.80 | – | – | not by 1,500 (§4.6) |
| Qwen2.5-3B LoRA | medical | 0.98 | 0.87 | 0.85 | 0.83 | – | – | not by 1,000 (§4.6) |

![Preservation trajectories](figures/fig1_preservation_trajectories.png)
![Preservation vs size](figures/fig5_preservation_vs_size.png)
![Recipe ablation](figures/fig6_recipe_ablation.png)

**Observations.**
- **Larger models drift less.** At matched steps preservation increases with size within each family. In Qwen
  on medical text, step 500 gives 0.79, 0.82 and 0.85, and step 1,000 gives 0.76, 0.80 and 0.83 for 0.5B, 1.5B
  and 3B. Pythia-410M is far more stable than 160M.
- **Sub-1B is not sufficient for a fast crossing.** Only Pythia-160M crossed 0.5 within 500 steps. Qwen2.5-0.5B
  (494M parameters) stayed above 0.71 for 3,000 steps.
- **Update size dominates.** A 5× larger LoRA learning rate on the same 0.5B model moved the 0.5 crossing from
  "never" to ~420–500 steps. In Pythia-160M, full fine-tuning at lr 1e-5 drifted far *less* than LoRA at 2e-4.
  So "steps until forgetting geometry" is not a property of model size alone.
- **Most drift happens early.** Most of the preservation loss occurs in the first ~100 steps, after which the
  curve flattens on a log-step axis.
- **The result is robust to the metric variant.** Mean-centred kNN gives values within ±0.03 of raw kNN, and
  k = 5/20 give the same ordering. At the middle layer preservation is 0.03–0.08 higher, with the same ordering
  and crossing pattern (`results/analysis/h1_mid_layer.csv`).
- **The domain-free control drifts too.** Fine-tuning on WikiText itself drifts about as much as the domain runs
  (Qwen-0.5B: 0.76 at 3,000 steps), so much of the drift is caused by fine-tuning itself, not by domain shift.

### 4.2 H2 – Isotropy

![Isotropy](figures/fig2_isotropy.png)

Final layer, general probes, 20 runs:

| Measure | runs monotonically more anisotropic | runs net more anisotropic at last step | median relative change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean pairwise cosine (↑ = anisotropic) | 0 / 20 | 12 / 20 | +1.7 % |
| IsoScore (↓ = anisotropic) | 0 / 20 | 16 / 20 | −7.0 % |
| Effective rank (↓ = anisotropic) | 0 / 20 | 15 / 20 | −4.9 % |

There is a weak net drift toward anisotropy, but it is not monotone in any run. Pythia-160M LoRA runs first
become markedly *more* isotropic (IsoScore up to 1.6× at steps 100–500) and then fall back. Mean cosine changes
by only a few percent, which is small next to the 15–75 % changes in kNN preservation. **H2 is not supported.**

### 4.3 H3 – Does a 60 % preservation threshold mark the onset of forgetting?

![Preservation vs forgetting](figures/fig3_preservation_vs_forgetting.png)

Pooled over all checkpoints (n = 313):

| | preservation ≥ 0.6 (n = 228) | preservation < 0.6 (n = 85) |
|---|---|---|
| mean Δ GK accuracy | −2.0 pp | −8.7 pp |
| share of checkpoints with a significant GK decline (McNemar p < .05) | 35 % | 81 % |

- The difference between the two groups is significant (Mann–Whitney p = 1e-13). Preservation correlates with
  Δ GK (Spearman ρ = 0.70) and very strongly with Δ WikiText NLL (ρ = −0.88).
- But this pooled association is mostly a difference *between* model families and recipes. It does not reflect
  a threshold within any single run.
- Per run, the first checkpoint with a significant GK decline occurred at:

| Run | step of first significant decline | preservation at that point |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen-0.5B medical (seeds 1/2/3) | 500 / 400 / 750 | 0.79 / 0.80 / 0.77 |
| Qwen-0.5B general | 100 | 0.81 |
| Qwen-1.5B medical | 50 | 0.90 |
| Qwen-3B medical | 200 | 0.84 |
| Qwen-0.5B lr 1e-3 (medical / code) | 50 / 100 | 0.78 / 0.78 |
| Pythia-160M LoRA | 100–300 | 0.43–0.50 |
| Pythia-410M (medical / code) | 150 / 500 | 0.79 / 0.81 |

- **Qwen models forget long before 0.6.** They lose general knowledge while preservation is still 0.77–0.90.
  Qwen-0.5B lost 8.8 pp GK (−8.2 pp MMLU) after 3,000 medical steps, and 9.9 pp after 3,000 *WikiText* steps.
  Yet preservation stayed ≥ 0.73.
- **Pythia-160M fits the threshold story only loosely.** Preservation crosses 0.6 (at ~70–100 steps) shortly
  before the first significant ARC decline (100–300 steps). But its MMLU is at chance (~23 %), so its GK signal
  is ARC only.
- **The same preservation means very different forgetting across recipes.**
  - Qwen-0.5B at lr 1e-3 reaches preservation ≈ 0.25 with −30 pp GK.
  - Pythia-160M at a similar preservation (0.25–0.3) shows only −4 pp.
  - So preservation is not calibrated across models.
- **WikiText NLL is the exception.** Its relationship with preservation is tight and almost model-independent
  (Fig. 3, right). Losing general-text neighbourhood structure goes hand in hand with losing general-text
  language modelling. The exception is the WikiText-control run, where NLL *improves* while preservation still
  drops.

**H3 is not supported as stated.** Preservation is associated with forgetting, but there is no
"onset at 60 %" threshold. For the Qwen family, accuracy starts falling at ≈ 0.8.

### 4.4 H4 – Medical vs code

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| Matched checkpoints (model, method, seed, step) | 128 |
| Mean preservation, medical − code | **−0.039** (Wilcoxon p = 1e-9); medical higher at 19 % of checkpoints |
| Mean Δ CKA, medical − code | −0.009 (p = 4e-9) |
| Mean Δ GK accuracy, medical − code | −1.4 pp (p = 8e-8): medical forgets *more* |
| Mean Δ WikiText NLL, medical − code | +0.21 nats (p = 4e-15): medical forgets *more* |

At 3,000 steps, per run:

| Model | medical | code |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen-0.5B (seeds 1/2/3) | 0.74 / 0.71 / 0.74 | 0.82 / 0.81 / 0.81 |
| Qwen-0.5B lr 1e-3 | 0.22 | 0.27 |
| Pythia-410M | 0.71 | 0.74 |
| Pythia-160M LoRA (seeds 1/2) | **0.28 / 0.35** | 0.25 / 0.30 |
| Pythia-160M full FT | **0.62** | 0.51 |

Only the Pythia-160M runs (bold) follow H4's direction.

Vocabulary overlap with general text (`results/corpus_stats.json`; reference = WikiText-103, ~2M Qwen tokens
per corpus):

| Corpus | token-unigram JSD vs WikiText (bits) | token mass in top-10k WikiText tokens | word-type coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| medical | 0.45 | 67 % | 90 % |
| code | 0.63 | 36 % | 80 % |
| general (split-half floor) | 0.01 | 91 % | 97 % |

Familiarity to the base model (step-0 NLL on held-out domain text, nats/token):

| Model | code | medical |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen-0.5B | 1.58 | 2.34 |
| Pythia-160M | 2.17 | 3.13 |
| Pythia-410M | 1.55 | 2.34 |

**Interpretation.**
- The premise of H4 holds: clinical notes share far more vocabulary with general text than code does.
- The conclusion does not. For most models, code fine-tuning preserved general-text geometry and general
  knowledge *better*.
- A plausible explanation is interference. Code tokens and contexts may occupy a largely separate region of
  representation space, so code updates disturb natural-language prose representations less. Clinical prose, by
  contrast, uses the same English token space, so its updates rewrite the same features general text relies on.
- Code is also much better modelled by the base models (lower NLL), so there is less to learn. In-domain loss
  fell less for code (Qwen-0.5B: 1.58 → ~1.35) than for medical (2.34 → ~1.75).
- The smallest model (Pythia-160M) behaves the other way, so the effect depends on scale.
- **H4 is not supported**; the opposite holds for 4 of the 5 model/recipe groups.

Fine-tuning moves in-domain neighbourhoods more than general ones in the expected direction: under medical
fine-tuning, medical-probe preservation is the lowest of the three probe sets for Qwen models
(`results/analysis/probe_set_preservation_at_max_step.csv`).

### 4.5 Learning actually happened

In-domain NLL fell in every run (Qwen-0.5B medical: 2.33 → 1.75 nats/token at 3,000 steps). WikiText-control
runs reduced WikiText NLL (Qwen-0.5B: 3.00 → 2.77). So the drift is not an artefact of failed training.

### 4.6 Truncated large-model runs

Status at the freeze at 15:45: Qwen-1.5B medical reached step 1,500 and Qwen-3B medical reached step 1,000.
Qwen-1.5B code and all 7B runs could not be completed (§6). The large-model rows therefore cover fewer steps.
Across the steps they do cover, they are consistently more stable than the smaller models.

## 5. Analysis & Discussion

**Scale.** Within one family and one recipe, bigger models keep more of their geometry, in line with the
direction of H1. But the specific numbers in H1 do not hold up.
- The "< 50 % within 500 steps for sub-1B" claim depends on the model: true for Pythia-160M, false for
  Qwen2.5-0.5B.
- It depends even more on update magnitude: learning rate, LoRA vs full fine-tuning.
- With a standard LoRA recipe, a well-trained ~0.5B model settles at 0.7–0.8 preservation instead of collapsing.
- Extrapolating the 1.5B/3B curves, which flatten at ≈ 0.8 on a log-step axis, a 7B model at this recipe would
  very likely stay well above 0.5 beyond 2,000 steps. That would match the 7B clause of H1, but trivially, since
  the 0.5B model does too. We did not measure 7B.

**Early warning.** Preservation is informative: it tracks general-text perplexity damage almost
deterministically. But accuracy-based forgetting starts while preservation is still high, and the
preservation→forgetting mapping differs between model families and learning rates. A useful early-warning rule
would therefore be relative and calibrated: for example, flag a fine-tuning run once preservation falls more
than X below its own short-horizon plateau, or use the probe-set NLL directly. A universal absolute threshold
such as 0.6 would not work.

**Isotropy.** Global isotropy statistics barely move and fluctuate in sign. Fine-tuning reshuffles local
neighbourhoods long before it changes the global shape of the space, so isotropy is a poor drift signal compared
with kNN preservation or CKA.

**Domain.** Lexical overlap with pretraining-like text did not predict geometric preservation. If anything,
*sharing* the representational substrate with general text (as clinical English does) causes more interference
with general-text geometry than a domain that lives in its own region (code).

**Surprises.**
1. The general-text control (WikiText) caused as much drift as domain fine-tuning, and *more* MMLU loss for
   Qwen-0.5B (−11 pp). Plain LM training on encyclopedic prose appears to erode the base model's multiple-choice
   answering format, which Qwen2.5 base models were partly trained for. MMLU-style forgetting therefore partly
   reflects format and skill, not just knowledge.
2. Full fine-tuning at a typical full-FT learning rate preserved geometry better than LoRA at a typical LoRA
   learning rate (Pythia-160M).

## 6. Limitations

- **No 7B results.** The 7B run started on the one large GPU slice but OOM'd when another user's job grew. A
  restart could not get enough memory, and at the measured ~7 s/step plus 8.5 min per evaluation it would not
  have finished in the session. Qwen-1.5B/3B trajectories are truncated (1,500 / 1,000 steps), and Qwen-1.5B and
  3B have no code-domain runs, so H4 at those sizes is untested.
- **One recipe per size.** Learning rate, LoRA rank and method strongly change drift speed, and only partial
  ablations were run (one model each). The step-based claims in H1 are not meaningful without fixing the
  recipe.
- **Seeds.** Three seeds were run only for Qwen-0.5B medical and code, and two for Pythia-160M. The seed sd is
  small (≤ 0.016 for Qwen-0.5B; up to ~0.09 for Pythia-160M, whose curves are noisy).
- **Probe design.** Mean-pooled 128-token probes from WikiText are one choice among many. Token-level or
  word-embedding neighbourhoods may behave differently. Under LoRA the input embedding matrix never changes, so
  only contextual geometry was meaningful here.
- **General-knowledge evaluation.** MMLU 0-shot with letter scoring is near chance for Pythia, so their GK
  signal is ARC-Easy only. 1,070 items give ±~2.5 pp sampling noise for a single checkpoint (mitigated by paired
  McNemar tests).
- **Vocabulary overlap is approximate.** It is measured against WikiText as a proxy for pretraining data; the
  real Qwen/Pythia pretraining corpora were not available. The medical corpus is synthetic (LLM-generated)
  clinical notes, which may be more "LM-like" than real clinical text.
- **Shared GPUs.** Runs had to be scheduled opportunistically. This affects only speed, not results; training
  order and data are seeded.

## 7. Conclusions & Next Steps

Fine-tuning reshapes the local neighbourhood structure of LM representations quickly. Most of the change
happens in the first ~100 steps, and larger models change less. But the specific predictions in the hypothesis
fail:
- The 50 % crossing depends more on training recipe and model family than on a sub-1B vs 7B split.
- Isotropy does not decline monotonically.
- General-knowledge forgetting starts while neighbourhood preservation is still ~0.8, not at 0.6.
- Code fine-tuning, not medical, preserves more general-text geometry for most models, despite lower lexical
  overlap.

kNN preservation is a good label-free proxy for damage to general language modelling, but it needs per-family
calibration before it can serve as a forgetting alarm.

**Follow-ups.**
1. Complete the 7B and 1.5B/3B code runs on dedicated hardware.
2. Sweep learning rate × size to fit "steps to cross" as a function of update norm.
3. Compare probe-set NLL with kNN preservation as early-warning signals.
4. Test real (non-synthetic) clinical text and multiple code languages.
5. Test whether replay or regularisation (e.g. L2-SP) keeps preservation and accuracy coupled.

## References / Resources

- Models: Qwen2.5-{0.5,1.5,3}B (Qwen team, 2024); Pythia-{160M,410M} (Biderman et al., 2023).
- Data: Asclepius Synthetic Clinical Notes (Kweon et al., 2024); codeparrot-clean-valid; WikiText-103 (Merity et
  al., 2016); MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021); ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018).
- Metrics: IsoScore (Rudman et al., 2022); anisotropy (Ethayarajh, 2019); linear CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019).
- Related: Merchant et al. 2020 (BERT fine-tuning geometry); Biderman et al. 2024 (LoRA learns less and forgets
  less); Luo et al. 2023 (forgetting in LLM continual fine-tuning).
- Code: `src/` (this workspace); outputs: `results/`, `figures/`.

Update 2026-10-22 (embedding_drift_finetuning workspace, LoRA fine-tuning 160M–7B on shared GPUs):
- A fully free GPU (48 GB) at session start was reservable with a tiny holder (`torch.empty(36GB)` + exit on a RELEASE file) while code was written; have the training script touch RELEASE after loading weights to CPU, just before `.cuda()`. But whatever you don't hold gets taken within minutes, and the 7B LoRA run (17 GB) still OOM'd mid-run when co-tenants grew — budget 7B training as infeasible unless a GPU is dedicated. On a GPU at 100% util shared with another user, 7B LoRA bs4×512 ran ~7 s/step; 3B 4.6 s/step; 1.5B 2.9 s/step; checkpoint evals (1.6k probes + 1,070 MCQ items) 4–8.5 min. 0.5B LoRA fits a 5 GB slice (2.4 GB peak, 20 min/3k steps); 1.5B peaks 4.5 GB.
- "Idle" 5–6 GB slices at 0% util are transient: other users' 41–43 GB jobs regrow and OOM you minutes later.
- Worker queue bug: a worker that retries the first unclaimed job starves smaller jobs if that job never fits → per-job memory need + skip; and when killing a worker loop, its job lock dir is orphaned (rmdir it). Writing reps before accuracy evals means a mid-eval kill leaves a checkpoint with reps but no metrics — filter to steps present in metrics.jsonl.

content.text:
The research is done: REPORT.md and README.md hold the actual results from 22 completed fine-tuning runs. None of the four parts of the hypothesis holds as stated. The 7B comparison could not be run: the shared GPUs never had enough free memory to finish it.

**Setup.** I used five base models: Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B and Pythia 160M/410M. Each was fine-tuned on clinical notes, Python code, or WikiText (a no-domain-shift control) for up to 3,000 steps. At 17 checkpoints I measured how much of the original neighbourhood structure of 1,000 fixed general-text passages survives (10 nearest neighbours), plus isotropy, MMLU + ARC-Easy accuracy, and perplexity. There were no API keys, so everything ran on local models.

**Findings against the hypothesis:**
- **H1 (fast collapse below 1B, slow at 7B): right direction, wrong specifics.** Bigger models do keep more structure. At step 500 preservation was 0.42 (160M), 0.74 (410M), 0.79 (0.5B), 0.82 (1.5B) and 0.85 (3B).
  - Qwen-0.5B never fell below 0.71 in 3,000 steps at the standard learning rate. At 5× that rate it crossed 0.5 after about 420–500 steps.
  - All 7 runs that ended below 0.5 also had in-domain loss going *up*, meaning the training itself was going wrong.
  - Every run that actually learned its domain ended between 0.57 and 0.82.
- **H2 (isotropy falls steadily): not supported.** No run (0 of 22) moved monotonically on any of the three isotropy measures, and the net changes were small (median IsoScore −8 %).
- **H3 (accuracy starts dropping below 60 % preservation): not supported.** Preservation does track forgetting overall (Spearman ρ = 0.69 with accuracy change, −0.90 with perplexity change). But in 16 of 21 runs accuracy dropped significantly while preservation was still at or above 0.6, usually around 0.77–0.90. A fixed 0.6 alarm would fire far too late.
- **H4 (medical preserves more than code): the reverse.** Code fine-tuning kept more structure at most matched checkpoints (difference −0.043, p = 3e-12), and medical caused more forgetting. This held even though the clinical notes share far more vocabulary with general text.
  - Caveat: code fine-tuning never reduced code loss, because these models already handle code well. So "code preserves more" partly just means "code training changed less".

**Limitations:**
- **No 7B result.** The 7B run started but ran out of memory when another user's job grew. The 1.5B and 3B medical runs were stopped at steps 2,500 and 1,500.
- **No code runs at 1.5B or 3B**, so the medical-vs-code comparison only covers models up to 0.5B.
- **Ablations are on one model each.** The learning-rate sweep was run only on Qwen-0.5B and full fine-tuning only on Pythia-160M.

I stopped all my GPU jobs at the end so nothing keeps using the shared machine. I did not commit anything to git. I also added notes from this session to my memory file on this host (GPU timings, the queueing pitfalls, and the need to always log in-domain loss).

Files are in the workspace:
- REPORT.md
- README.md
- planning.md
- src/ (code)
- results/analysis/ (tables)
- figures/ (fig1–fig6)
